claims.text: The starting protective coating contains mixed FCC and BCC phases.
Conventional deposition produces loosely bonded or non-optimized transitional regions between the coating and substrate.
Introducing an optimized nickel-based transition layer produces a graded coating–substrate interface.
Spraying distance and scanning speed can be optimized to form the proposed nickel-based transition layer.
The graded interface produces residual compressive stresses.
The transition layer refines the coating or interface grain structure.
The transition layer reduces dislocation mobility.
The engineered transition layer stabilizes the phase structure by impeding dislocation glide and climb.
Suppression of dislocation nucleation and motion delays creep-strain initiation and lowers the steady-state creep rate.
The transition layer prevents early-stage phase coarsening that would otherwise weaken the coating.
At approximately 800 °C under continuous loading, the transition-layer coating will have a significantly lower steady-state creep strain rate than a coating without the tailored layer.
The transition-layer coating will have higher microhardness than the baseline coating.
The transition-layer coating will retain a more stable microstructure than the baseline coating during sustained loading.
A coating without the specialized nickel-based layer has less optimized interfacial bonding and microstructural refinement.
Approximately 800 °C is an applicable elevated-temperature operating condition for studying these coatings.
Dislocation motion and phase coarsening dominate creep behavior near 800 °C in the proposed coating.
The hypothesis may not apply outside the stress and temperature range typical of these coatings.
Prior evidence shows that a suitable nickel-based transition layer can improve coating–substrate bonding and resistance to cracking under bending loads.
The magnitude of creep-rate reduction and long-term microstructural stability remain unquantified.
Failure to observe a statistically significant creep-rate reduction, hardness improvement, or greater microstructural stability relative to the no-layer control would falsify the hypothesis.
